primary_cause: Crude fell about 5% on Mar 27 and logged fifth straight weekly loss as COVID demand destruction overwhelmed stimulus optimism. No major ConocoPhillips-specific negative release. Renewed oil-price collapse
secondary_factors: Ongoing Russia-Saudi price war. Recession fears. COP basically trading as oil beta
store_description: COP was basically trading as an oil beta. With WTI and Brent under renewed pressure and the market concluding that a $2.2T U.S. stimulus package would not quickly restore fuel demand E&P names like COP sold off harder than the broad tape.

primary_cause: Mar 26 U.S. jobless-claims report showed record 3.3M initial claims intensifying fears of credit-card delinquencies and consumer loan losses. No fresh Capital One-specific release. Worsening expected consumer credit losses
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Uncertainty around payment deferrals and forbearance economics
store_description: Capital One had heavy exposure to credit cards and unsecured consumer lending so the record claims number was a direct hit to the market loss assumptions. This looked more like a COF-specific balance-sheet sensitivity selloff than a generic market decline.

primary_cause: No Cisco press release or Reuters item in prior 3 days. Worsening enterprise-spending concern as virus shock spread and March data deteriorated. Anticipated slowdown in enterprise and networking spend
secondary_factors: Broad tech de-risking after sharp stimulus rally. Concern hardware demand and customer budgets would weaken
store_description: Unlike some later 2020 CSCO moves this March 27 decline does not appear tied to a discrete company announcement. The cleaner explanation is that investors were marking down cyclical enterprise tech names as the economic shutdown deepened.

primary_cause: Boeing still dealing with simultaneous COVID air-travel collapse and unresolved 737 MAX damage. Market focused on Boeing push for government support and liquidity. Boeing Mar 27 release was benign. Ongoing liquidity and demand fears in commercial aerospace
secondary_factors: 737 MAX overhang. Concern over government-aid terms
store_description: By March 30 investors were effectively valuing Boeing through a survival and liquidity lens rather than on near-term earnings with airlines grounding fleets and deferring purchases. The stock 6% slide fits the market continuing skepticism that stimulus alone could offset the collapse in aircraft demand.

primary_cause: Simon had already temporarily closed all U.S. properties Mar 18. Mall REITs remained under pressure from rent-collection and tenant-survival fears. No fresh SPG-specific negative Mar 27-29. Ongoing mall-closure and tenant-default risk
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Concern around highly leveraged retail real estate
store_description: Even though the percentage drop was smaller than earlier March plunges SPG was still trading off the same core thesis: shut malls meant near-term rent disruption potential abatements and higher risk of retailer bankruptcies. The market treated mall landlords as structurally exposed to prolonged lockdowns.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mastercard had already updated Q1 outlook Mar 24 saying COVID causing further deterioration in cross-border volumes switched volumes and transaction metrics. Collapse in cross-border payment volume from global travel shutdowns
secondary_factors: Weaker consumer spending. Recession fears
store_description: This one does have a clear company-linked catalyst inside the window. Mastercard specifically warned that cross-border and transaction metrics had deteriorated further which mattered because cross-border spending is a high-margin revenue stream. The March 31 drop looks like the market continuing to price that damage.

primary_cause: No PepsiCo-specific negative release in prior 3 days. Mar 31 drop in U.S. consumer confidence to 120.0 from 132.6. Deepening concern away-from-home consumption channels would weaken
secondary_factors: Quarter-end rotation out of defensives. Uncertainty around foodservice exposure. Deteriorating consumer and restaurant and channel outlook
store_description: Pepsi was relatively defensive but investors were still reassessing demand across convenience vending stadium and foodservice channels as lockdowns spread. Without a fresh company headline this looks like macro and channel repricing.

primary_cause: Lam had provided business update Mar 17 warning COVID-19 affecting supply chain and demand visibility. No better company-specific Mar 28-30 headline. Semiconductor-equipment demand and supply-chain uncertainty from COVID
secondary_factors: Cyclical-tech de-risking. Customer capex concerns
store_description: Lam earlier update established that the company was not insulated from pandemic disruption and by March 31 investors were still reducing exposure to semiconductor capital equipment despite a few-day market rebound. The 6% move is consistent with elevated sensitivity to fab-spending uncertainty.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Nike had closed stores outside Asia-Pacific beginning Mar 15 and continued emphasizing COVID response measures. Store closures and collapsing discretionary retail demand
secondary_factors: Supply-chain disruption. Uncertainty about reopening timing. Digital demand was partial offset
store_description: Nike physical-store footprint and global consumer exposure made it an obvious pandemic loser in late March. By March 31 the market was still pricing lost in-store sales and a sharp revenue hit from extended closures even though digital demand was a partial offset.

primary_cause: No fresh Oracle-specific announcement in prior 3 days. Renewed selling in enterprise software tied to recession fears after Mar 31 consumer-confidence miss. Expected slowdown in enterprise software spending
secondary_factors: Quarter-end risk reduction. Fading momentum after stimulus bounce
store_description: Oracle had already reported earnings earlier in March so this late-March move does not line up with a new company event. It looks more like investors marking down mature enterprise software names on the view that new license and services activity would soften.

primary_cause: No fresh P&G-specific negative in prior 3 days. Mar 31 consumer confidence at lowest since July 2017. Macro and positioning rather than company news
secondary_factors: Quarter-end rebalancing after consumer staples had outperformed. Investors rotated out of some defensive winners
store_description: PG was not falling because of a new operational warning. If anything staples demand was holding up comparatively well. The size of the decline suggests factor rotation and broad-risk selling not a hidden company-specific shock.

primary_cause: Record Mar 26 jobless-claims spike and deepening recession fears pointed to higher loan-loss provisioning risk. No unique U.S. Bancorp headline. Expected credit losses and margin pressure
secondary_factors: Zero-rate environment. Concern over consumer and commercial forbearance programs
store_description: USB was seen as higher quality than some peers but it still had meaningful exposure to a rapidly deteriorating credit environment. The March 31 move fits sector-level repricing of bank earnings power and reserve needs.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Starbucks had shifted most U.S. stores to drive-thru-only and closed cafe access after employee pressure and COVID spread. Store-operating restrictions and demand disruption
secondary_factors: Labor-cost commitments. Uncertainty over how long mobility restrictions would last
store_description: This was not just a generic market move. Starbucks had materially changed its U.S. operating model which implied lower traffic execution friction and margin pressure even if many locations stayed partially open. That remained a live overhang on March 31.

primary_cause: No Southern-specific negative release in prior 3 days. Violent rotation and de-risking move in utilities amid quarter-end positioning. Broader concern about economic disruption and financing conditions
secondary_factors: Concern about commercial power demand. Capital-market conditions for utilities
store_description: SO drop was unusually large for a utility. No evidence of a discrete Southern catalyst so this looks more like a high-beta unwind in a stressed tape.

primary_cause: No AT&T release in prior 3 days. Advertising and media environment deteriorating sharply. Reuters estimating U.S. ad industry could lose nearly $26B or 10.6% in revenue. Worsening ad and media outlook layered onto general telecom defensives selling
secondary_factors: WarnerMedia exposure. Sports shutdowns. Recession fears
store_description: AT&T wireless business was comparatively defensive but its media assets were vulnerable to an advertising downturn and delayed content releases. In late March investors were increasingly treating T as more than just a stable telecom dividend story.

primary_cause: Freight and logistics networks facing major COVID disruptions especially in air cargo and international transport. No UPS-specific Mar 28-30 announcement. Worsening global shipping and operational disruption outlook
secondary_factors: Mix shift away from higher-margin segments. General industrial and recession fears
store_description: While e-commerce package volume was rising investors were also confronting severe dislocation in global freight and B2B shipping. The stock decline likely reflected concern that network stress and macro weakness would outweigh any residential-delivery benefit in the near term.

primary_cause: Record jobless claims and collapsing economic outlook kept pressure on banks with large consumer and corporate credit books. No fresh JPMorgan-specific headline. Rising credit-loss expectations
secondary_factors: Zero-rate net-interest-margin pressure. Uncertainty around loan relief programs
store_description: JPM was the strongest large U.S. bank operationally but even it could not escape the market need to reprice recessionary charge-offs. The March 31 drop fits continued revision of reserve and earnings expectations rather than a bank-specific bombshell.

primary_cause: Record 3.3M claims print and deteriorating macro backdrop. Wells Fargo weaker relative positioning made it especially exposed to renewed banking stress. Escalating credit-loss fears
secondary_factors: Low-rate pressure. Legacy operational constraints. Investor preference against weaker banks in crisis
store_description: Wells Fargo was already seen as less flexible than peers because of its existing regulatory baggage so the March labor shock hit sentiment harder. Absent a fresh company release the simplest explanation is sector stress plus WFC-specific fragility.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Mar 30 Raytheon and United Technologies said all regulatory approvals obtained and merger would close after Carrier and Otis separations on Apr 3. Nominally positive but stock fell as aerospace demand fears overwhelmed merger milestone. Civil-aerospace collapse
secondary_factors: Concern over exposure to Pratt & Whitney and aviation end markets. Broad industrial selling
store_description: The market viewed the merger closing as administratively positive but economically mistimed because it increased exposure to a commercial aerospace market in free fall. So the news was good on paper yet the stock still traded on pandemic-driven end-market damage.

primary_cause: No fresh Intuit-specific negative in prior 3 days. Severe stress on small businesses — surveys showing 96% of small business owners already feeling negative COVID effects. Worsening outlook for Intuit small-business ecosystem exposure
secondary_factors: General software de-risking. Recession fears
store_description: Intuit was more economically sensitive than many investors initially assumed because QuickBooks and adjacent services are tied to small-business formation payroll and survival. As the small-business outlook darkened into month-end the stock sold off accordingly.
